hints: Remember what an ideal gas assumes, that particles have no attractions and no volume, then ask which conditions make that most true.
Compare the two gases first: ammonia can hydrogen bond while neon is a tiny noble gas with only very weak London forces.
Now compare the temperatures and think how extra kinetic energy at high temperature helps particles overcome any attractions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a gas ideal**

Think of an ideal gas as particles that just bounce and never stick together. Real gases deviate when attractions pull them together or when they are squeezed slow and close.

Ideal conditions: high temperature, low pressure, small non-polar particles

**Compare the particle type: $\text{NH}_3$ vs $\text{Ne}$**

Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, so its molecules attract each other strongly. Neon, $\text{Ne}$, is a small monatomic noble gas with only very weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces.

$$\text{NH}_3 \text{ : strong attractions} > \text{Ne : very weak attractions}$$

**Compare the temperature: 100 K vs 500 K**

Low temperature means low kinetic energy, so slow particles can stick together and deviate more. High temperature means fast particles with lots of energy to overcome attractions and fly past each other.

$$\text{higher T = more ideal, lower T = less ideal}$$

**Put both factors together**

We want the weakest attractions plus the highest temperature. That is the small, non-polar neon at the hot 500 K temperature, where particles move fast and barely interact.

options.A: Worst choice. Ammonia has strong hydrogen bonding and at 100 K the particles are slow, so attractions dominate and deviation from ideal is greatest.
options.B: Better than A because 500 K gives more kinetic energy to overcome attractions, but ammonia is still polar with hydrogen bonding, so it still deviates significantly.
options.C: Good particle choice because neon has only very weak London forces, but 100 K is cold so particles are slow and even weak attractions cause some deviation.
options.D: Best choice. Neon is tiny and non-polar with minimal intermolecular forces, and at 500 K the particles have high kinetic energy so they move too fast to attract each other. This most closely matches ideal assumptions.
